item.title: Frequent co-occurring atmospheric phenomena amplify precipitation extremes
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02806-7

Observations and simulations show that concurrent atmospheric phenomena (CAP) dominate the greenhouse gas-driven amplification of extreme precipitation from 1980 to 2020. This increased frequency of CAP-related precipitation extremes accounts for 56–70% of extreme precipitation increases projected for 2060–2100 in Northern Hemisphere hotspots, driven by oceanic high-pressure anomalies that strengthen land–sea pressure gradients, alongside enhanced moisture convergence.

item.title: Climate change signals for adaptation action
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02814-7

Signals of climate change measured in physical and ecological systems are salient for adaptation, but are not currently directly usable. This Perspective aims to better connect early warning signals of climate change with the needs of adaptation planning and decision-making.

item.title: Tyre wear particles as important contributors to cryosphere darkening
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02800-z

The abrasion of tyres leads to the emission of particulate matter to the atmosphere. Here the authors quantify the effect that these tyre wear particles have on snow and ice, showing that they contribute to melting in some regions.
